description: Our team is exploring the “Dancing with the SARS” challenge by building a dual‑purpose platform that blends science, data, and play. In Phase 1, we aim to create a simple interactive game where users adjust variables such as deforestation or urbanization and instantly see the impacts on climate and agriculture across regions.
summary:
TerraPulse is an interactive Earth-observation and environmental intelligence platform that transforms satellite data into accessible insights about our changing planet. Using The Gambia as its pilot study area, the project focuses on monitoring two critical natural resources: forests and water bodies.

By aiming to integrate NASA's NISAR radar observations with complementary datasets from Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, ESA WorldCover, and the JRC Global Surface Water dataset, TerraPulse aims to help users explore environmental changes across locations and time periods through interactive maps and satellite imagery (and graphs).

Addressing the *Dancing with the SARS* challenge, TerraPulse demonstrates how radar remote sensing and geospatial technologies can reveal changes that might otherwise go unnoticed. Its innovation lies in bringing multiple Earth-observation datasets together within an accessible, interactive platform that connects scientific data with real-world environmental issues.

Beyond visualization, TerraPulse aspires to empower researchers, conservationists, policymakers, and communities with evidence to support environmental monitoring, resource management, and informed decision-making. There is the possibility of including an AI assistant that will break down the trends and give analysis in plain language. Ultimately, it bridges the gap between complex satellite observations and meaningful action towards a more sustainable future.
details:
TerraPulse is an interactive Earth-observation and environmental intelligence platform designed to help users explore, monitor and understand changes in the Earth's natural environment using satellite data and geospatial technologies.

Using The Gambia as its pilot study area, the platform focuses on forests and water bodies, including vegetation, mangroves, wetlands and surface water. NASA's NISAR mission, particularly its L-band and S-band radar observations, is our primary data source, complemented by datasets such as Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, ESA WorldCover and JRC Global Surface Water. Our vision is to enable users to explore different environmental features, compare observations across dates and identify changes over time.

TerraPulse aims to make satellite data more accessible and understandable, particularly for people without specialist knowledge of remote sensing or GIS. It can serve as a resource for environmental research, conservation, policymaking and education. By visualising environmental changes, the platform can help users better understand the consequences of human activities and support more informed decisions about natural resource management.

Our ambition is to move beyond simply showing where environmental changes occur to helping people understand why they matter and how different environmental processes influence one another. For example, we want users to explore relationships between deforestation and local temperatures, mangrove loss and aquatic life, urbanisation and agricultural land loss, and vegetation loss and soil degradation. Starting with The Gambia, we envision a platform that can eventually be applied globally.

We used Lovable to build the initial platform which includes TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS and JSON, with React for frontend development and Node.js for backend development. Other technologies and resources include OpenStreetMap, NASA Earthdata, and REST APIs. Github was used for deployment.

TerraPulse combines three functions: environmental monitoring, scientific visualisation and interactive learning. Beyond observing environmental changes, we envision an interactive simulation feature that allows users to adjust parameters such as deforestation and urbanisation and explore their potential effects on other environmental conditions. This encourages experimentation and helps communicate complex environmental relationships in an engaging way.

Our decisions were influenced by the relevance of environmental issues in The Gambia, satellite data availability, the technical complexity of radar data processing, accessibility for non-specialists, scalability and our limited development time and resources.

An important part of our journey is that both team members are self-taught beginner programmers. We embraced the challenge as an opportunity to learn unfamiliar technologies and develop a solution beyond our existing technical experience. Although the current version is an early prototype, it establishes the foundation for our vision of transforming satellite observations into accessible environmental intelligence that supports awareness, research and sustainable decision-making.
